extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, scientists, and educated general readers interested in comparative psychology and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of mental capacities in non-human animals (imitation, attention, memory, imagination, reason, abstraction, language, tool-use, etc.) using observational and anecdotal evidence to compare them with human faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMITATION
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of IMITATION is strong in man, and especially, as I have myself observed, with savages. ... no animal voluntarily imitates an action performed by man, until in the ascending scale we come to monkeys, which are well known to be ridiculous mockers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counterexamples: wolves reared by dogs learned to bark; parrots imitate sounds they often hear; a dog reared by a cat learnt the cat's licking action; kittens copying a mother's trick of putting paws into narrow-mouthed jugs. Note the distinction between voluntary imitation of man and interspecific imitation. Use reports of repeated, confirmatory observations to infer imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: PARENTAL EDUCATION / TEACHING
rubrics_metrics.description: The parents of many animals, trusting to the principle of imitation in their young, and more especially to their instinctive or inherited tendencies, may be said to educate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed behaviours where parents progressively expose young to increasing difficulty (e.g. hawks dropping dead then live prey to teach hunting) count as teaching. Cite specific, detailed observations to infer parental instruction rather than mere instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATTENTION
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardly any faculty is more important for the intellectual progress of man than ATTENTION. Animals clearly manifest this power, as when a cat watches by a hole and prepares to spring on its prey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure variability of attention across individuals and species (example: monkey-actors selected for ability to sustain attention; inattentive animals are harder to train). Use distractibility and trainability as indicators of attention strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: MEMORY
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals have excellent MEMORIES for persons and places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long-interval recognition examples (baboon recognizing after nine months; dog recognizing owner after five years) and social-recognition evidence (ants recognizing nestmates after months) to demonstrate memory for individuals, places, and temporal intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMAGINATION
rubrics_metrics.description: The IMAGINATION is one of the highest prerogatives of man. ... As dogs, cats, horses, and probably all the higher animals, even birds, have vivid dreams, and this is shewn by their movements and the sounds uttered, we must admit that they possess some power of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer imagination from dream-like behaviours (movements and vocalizations during sleep), from apparent conjuring of 'fantastic images' (e.g. dogs baying at night), and from behaviour that suggests internally generated images affecting action.

rubrics_metrics.name: REASON
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the faculties of the human mind, it will, I presume, be admitted that REASON stands at the summit. Only a few persons now dispute that animals possess some power of reasoning. Animals may constantly be seen to pause, deliberate, and resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify acts of deliberation and problem-solving that are unlikely to be mere instinct or chance (examples: dogs diverging on thin ice possibly to distribute weight; elephants and bears creating currents to bring objects within reach; retrievers killing one bird to carry both). Use repeated, independently witnessed incidents as evidence of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASSOCIATION OF IDEAS / LEARNING FROM EXPERIENCE
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only judge by the circumstances under which actions are performed, whether they are due to instinct, or to reason, or to the mere association of ideas: this latter principle, however, is intimately connected with reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a pike repeatedly stunned by dashed against glass eventually learned caution (association of shock with attempting to catch fish behind glass); monkeys after a single sting hold packets to their ear. Use changes in behaviour after single or repeated adverse/beneficial events to infer association-based learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: USE OF TOOLS / IMPLEMENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: It has often been said that no animal uses any tool; but the chimpanzee in a state of nature cracks a native fruit... monkeys use stones and sticks as implements; elephants break off branches to drive away flies; orangs use sticks as levers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish opportunistic use of objects as tools from deliberate fashioning. Observe transfer of tool-use to novel tasks (e.g. monkey using stone to open other nuts, using stick as lever) and independent invention vs learning from conspecifics. Repeated, natural observations strengthen the case for tool-use.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROPENSITY TO FASHION IMPLEMENTS (manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fashioning of an implement for a special purpose is absolutely peculiar to man (as claimed by some); but it is plausible that breaking flints accidentally could lead to deliberate breaking and then to rude fashioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether observed tool modifications represent purposeful manufacture or accidental flaking later co-opted. Consider archaeological/longitudinal evidence (time and gradual refinement) and comparisons with non-human instances of intentional shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDEA OF PROPERTY
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Zoological Gardens, a monkey, which had weak teeth, used to break open nuts with a stone; after using the stone, he hid it in the straw, and would not let any other monkey touch it. Here, then, we have the idea of property; but this idea is common to every dog with a bone, and to most or all birds with their nests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guarding/hiding of objects and possessive behaviours (dogs with bones, birds with nests, monkey hiding a stone) as indicators of a sense of property. Distinguish transitory possession from durable property concept by testing refusal to share and defence across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROGRESSIVE IMPROVEMENT / CULTURAL TRANSMISSION
rubrics_metrics.description: That man alone is capable of progressive improvement... admits of no dispute; and this is mainly due to his power of speaking and handing down his acquired knowledge. With animals... young learn caution by seeing their brethren caught or poisoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether behaviours spread and persist across generations via social learning (examples: birds learning to avoid telegraph wires over a few years; increased wariness of fur-bearing animals in hunting regions). Consider the role of communication (language) in cumulative cultural transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABSTRACTION / GENERAL CONCEPTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest stress seems to be laid on the supposed entire absence in animals of the power of abstraction, or of forming general concepts. But when a dog sees another dog at a distance, it is often clear that he perceives that it is a dog in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer abstraction from behaviour indicating recognition of a class (e.g. a dog's sudden change of manner upon recognizing a dog as friend). Use behaviour showing generalized expectations (searching for 'something' after a cue) as evidence that animals form general concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: SELF-CONSCIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be freely admitted that no animal is self-conscious, if by this term it is implied that he reflects on such points as whence he comes or whither he will go, or what is life and death. But how can we feel sure that an old dog... never reflects on his past pleasures or pains in the chase? And this would be a form of self-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish high-level reflective self-consciousness (philosophical reflection on existence) from lower forms (memory of past events, reflection on experiences). Use indirect inferences from memory, anticipatory behaviour, and affective states; avoid overclaiming from sparse data.

rubrics_metrics.name: MENTAL INDIVIDUALITY / CONTINUITY OF CONSCIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals retain their mental individuality... When my voice awakened a train of old associations in the mind of the before-mentioned dog, he must have retained his mental individuality, although every atom of his brain had probably undergone change more than once during the interval of five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long-term behavioural continuity and identity-preserving responses (recognition after years) as evidence for mental individuality. Consider philosophical objections but rely on observed continuity of associative patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: LANGUAGE (ARTICULATE VS INARTICULATE) AND SYMBOLIC ASSOCIATION
rubrics_metrics.description: The habitual use of articulate language is, however, peculiar to man; but man is not the only animal that can make use of language to express what is passing in his mind, and can understand, more or less, what is so expressed by another. ... The lower animals differ from man solely in his almost infinitely larger power of associating together the most diversified sounds and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) inarticulate cries and gestures expressing emotion (shared with animals), (b) learned association of sounds/words with objects/people (parrots, dogs), and (c) habitual articulate language unique to humans. Use clear cases of word-object/person associations (parrots naming people, dogs responding to phrases) and learned song transmission in birds as evidence of symbolic association.

rubrics_metrics.name: DISTINGUISHING INSTINCT FROM REASON
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only judge by the circumstances under which actions are performed, whether they are due to instinct, or to reason, or to the mere association of ideas: this latter principle, however, is intimately connected with reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze context, novelty of situation, flexibility of response, and whether behaviour could be adaptive instinct or learned/inferential. Use controlled observation of novel problems (e.g. elephants using sticks to reach objects) and consider alternative explanations before attributing reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: CAUTION / SAGACITY AS ADAPTIVE LEARNING
rubrics_metrics.description: Where trapping has long been carried on, the animals exhibit an almost incredible amount of sagacity, caution and cunning... young in hunted districts are more wary than old ones where they are not much disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geographic and temporal comparisons (regions with long hunting pressure vs naive regions) and observations of behavioral shifts (avoidance of traps, wires) to infer acquired caution and cleverness. Consider both individual learning and possible inherited changes over generations.
